facts.fact_text: On 19 February 2008 a presidential election was held in Armenia.
The applicant was an active supporter of Mr Ter-Petrosyan's candidacy in the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election.

Immediately after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election, Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square (also known as Opera Square) in central Yerevan to protest against alleged irregularities in the election process.
Mr Ter-Petrosyan announced that the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election had not been free and fair.
From 20 February 2008 onwards, nationwide daily protest rallies were held by Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters, with their main meeting place being Freedom Square and the surrounding park in Yerevan.
The rallies at Freedom Square, held during the daytime and late into the night, attracted at times tens of thousands of people.
Several hundred demonstrators stayed at Freedom Square around the clock, having set up a camp.
The applicant was an active participant in the rallies at Freedom Square and was often on the podium.
The applicant made a speech on the first day of the rallies at Freedom Square.
On 29 February 2008 the rallies at Freedom Square were still in full swing.
On the night of 29 February 2008 the applicant camped at Freedom Square.
The applicant alleged that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m. the police arrived at Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that the several hundred demonstrators camping at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 were mostly still asleep when the police arrived, although some were awake, having been informed in advance about the arrival of a large number of police officers.

The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was also at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 and addressed the demonstrators, saying: "We see that police forces have arrived at the square. Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".
The Government contested the applicant's allegations regarding the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square.

The Government claimed that the reason for the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square was information obtained on 29 February 2008 by the Armenian Police and National Security Service, according to which a large number of weapons, including metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives, were to be distributed to the protesters to incite provocative actions and mass disorder in Yerevan on 1 March 2008.

The Government claimed that members of the relevant police force, without being equipped with any protective gear, arrived at Freedom Square where about 800 to 900 demonstrators armed with metal rods and wooden clubs had gathered waiting for the police.

The Government claimed that the demonstrators attacked the police officers on 1 March 2008, hitting them and throwing stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails at them, as a result of which numerous police officers were injured.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.
The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that a number of participants in the mass events at Freedom Square illegally possessed and carried illegally obtained arms and ammunition.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant submitted that he had not committed any offence and had been participating in a peaceful demonstration at Freedom Square when, at around 6.30 a.m., thousands of police officers had started beating peaceful demonstrators with rubber batons without prior warning or orders to disperse.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant admitted his participation in the demonstrations and marches but stated that he had stayed at Freedom Square around the clock only on 29 February 2008.
During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that he had been up on the podium on multiple occasions but that the podium had been accessible to anyone.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that he had never seen the demonstrators with any weapons or ammunition, that the demonstrations had been peaceful and accompanied with song and dance, and that nobody had given any orders to resist the police.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that orders to resist the police would have been pointless anyway, since the police had entered the square covertly and started assaulting the demonstrators with rubber batons.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that from 20 February 2008 onwards the applicant, together with Mr Ter-Petrosyan and others, organised and conducted unlawful public events, mass demonstrations, 24-hour long rallies, assemblies, pickets and sit-ins disrupting the normal life, traffic, functioning of public and private institutions and peace and quiet of the population in Yerevan and involving calls for a violent overthrow of the government and public insults addressed at public officials connected with the performance of their official duties.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police officers demanded the participants in the demonstration at Freedom Square to give a possibility to verify the veracity of the information that they possessed arms and ammunition, and once again warned them to end the unlawful event, the applicant and other demonstrators, disobeying the police officers' lawful orders, committed life- and health-threatening assault on them.

In his complaint of 12 June 2008, the applicant submitted that he had participated in the demonstrations held from 20 February 2008 onwards, which had been held in compliance with the Constitution and Article 11 of the Convention and involved no criminal behaviour.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that from a formal point of view, the demonstration that lasted from 21 February to 1 March 2008 did not comply with the requirements of law because the Mayor of Yerevan had neither been notified nor taken note of a demonstration to be held.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted the OSCE/ODIHR report as stating: "From 21 February to early morning on 1 March protesters held a peaceful, though not formally authorised, assembly (and tent camp) in Freedom Square in Yerevan and conducted numerous peaceful processions. Speakers at the assembly announced that their aim was to annul and repeat the election. Until 1 March, the authorities overall tolerated the protests."

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 intervention was justified with the argument that on 29 February the police and the National Security Service had received intelligence information according to which arms were building up at Freedom Square, and that in order to render the situation harmless, in the morning of 1 March the police undertook an operation intended to seize those socially-dangerous materials.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the campaign headquarters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan and the opposition Heritage Party both insisted that the objective of the measures of the morning of 1 March 2008 was, under the disguise of an inspection of the area, to terminate by force the peaceful demonstrations that had been ongoing for ten days, to remove the persons participating in the sit-in and to ban further demonstrations at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that while it is true that every day prior to 1 March the police announced over loudspeakers that the demonstration was unlawful and ordered the demonstrators to end it, no such order was made in the morning of 1 March 2008 and no time-limit was given to the demonstrators to end the demonstration as required by section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) stated that the violations and shortcomings observed in the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election raised questions among a part of the Armenian public with regard to the credibility of the outcome of the election, and that this lack of public confidence was the basis for the peaceful protests – held without prior official notification – that ensued after the announcement of the preliminary results, and which were tolerated by the authorities for ten days.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that opposition supporters began peaceful rallies on 20 February 2008 in Yerevan to protest against the election result and demand a rerun, and that on the evening of 1 March 2008, after eleven days of protest by opposition supporters, violence erupted when police moved into Freedom Square in central Yerevan to disperse the protesters camped out in tents, leaving eight people dead, including one police officer, and dozens injured.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that statements taken from demonstrators and bystanders suggested that the first police action in the early morning of 1 March 2008 against the Freedom Square tent encampment entailed excessive use of force, without warning and in the absence, at the start, of resistance.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that several witnesses interviewed separately by Human Rights Watch consistently described that some time shortly after 6 a.m. on 1 March 2008, while it was still dark, hundreds of Special Forces police in riot armour, with helmets, plastic shields, and rubber truncheons, started approaching Freedom Square from Tumanyan Street and Mashtots Avenue, surrounded the square and stood there for a few minutes.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to Mr Ter-Petrosyan's account, he addressed the protesters asking them to step back from the police line and then to stay where they were and wait for instructions from the police, and also warned the police that there were women and children among the demonstrators.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to multiple witnesses, even before Mr Ter-Petrosyan finished his address, police advanced towards the demonstrators in several lines, beating their truncheons against their plastic shields, making no audible demand for anyone to disperse nor giving any indication of the purpose of their presence, and then without any warning, riot police attacked the demonstrators, using rubber truncheons, iron sticks, and electric shock batons.
The applicant alleged that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m. the police arrived at Freedom Square.
The applicant alleged that in total about 800 heavily armed police officers appeared at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.
The applicant alleged that the police cordon started approaching the tents at Freedom Square and panic broke out among the demonstrators who started waking the others up.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.
The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was immediately arrested and taken away from Freedom Square on 1 March 2008.
The applicant alleged that within a few minutes no demonstrator remained at Freedom Square, since everybody, including the applicant, had tried to save themselves by fleeing.
The applicant alleged that he and other activists were then pursued by the police through the streets and arrested.

On 1 March 2008 the Special Investigative Service of Armenia instituted criminal case no. 62202508 under Article 225.1 §§ 1 and 2, Article 235 §§ 1 and 2 and Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code in connection with the events at Freedom Square.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

After Freedom Square was cleared of demonstrators on 1 March 2008, some of them relocated to the area near the French Embassy, the Yerevan Mayor's Office and the Yerevan Press Building, situated at Grigor Lusavorich and Arshakunyats Streets about 1.7-2 km from Freedom Square.
Following the events of 1 March 2008, a state of emergency was declared by the incumbent President Kocharyan.
The state of emergency declared by President Kocharyan prohibited, inter alia, the holding of any further rallies and other mass public events for a period of twenty days.

According to a handwritten document entitled "the record of bringing-in", the applicant was "brought in" to Kentron Police Station on 1 March 2008 at around 6.30 a.m. by three police officers, E.R., H.S. and A.A., from 1 Grigor Lusavorich Street.

The record of bringing-in stated that the applicant was brought to Kentron Police Station "for organising unauthorised demonstrations at Freedom Square in support of Mr Ter-Petrosyan, resisting police officers and disobeying their lawful orders".
The applicant alleged that in reality he had been taken into custody by about 10-15 persons who did not introduce themselves as police officers and were masked.
The applicant alleged that those persons had been pursuing him all the way from Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that he had managed to catch a taxi, but the taxi had been blocked after about 1-2 km by a police car at the intersection of Arshakunyats and Grigor Lusavorich Streets near the Yerevan Press Building.
The applicant alleged that the above-mentioned persons had forced him out of the taxi and started kicking, punching and hitting him with rubber batons.
The applicant alleged that he had then lost consciousness and been transported to Kentron Police Station.
The applicant alleged that upon his arrival at Kentron Police Station the same persons had continued to beat and humiliate him.

The applicant alleged that different parts of his body had been hit at Kentron Police Station, including his head and legs, as a result of which he had fallen on the floor, bleeding and unable to get up.
The applicant alleged that he had been hit on the head again at Kentron Police Station, which had resulted in concussion and loss of consciousness.

Police officer E.R. reported to the Chief of Kentron Police Station that at around 7.30 a.m. on 1 March 2008, together with police officers H.S. and A.A., he brought the applicant in to Kentron Police Station from near Yerevan circus for having resisted police officers.

Another report addressed by police officer E.R. to the Chief of Kentron Police Station, signed by all three officers E.R., H.S. and A.A., stated that following an alert received on 1 March 2008, they were in the area of the unauthorised demonstration held at Freedom Square where the demonstrators were ordered to terminate the unauthorised demonstration and to clear the square.

A memorandum signed by the Chief of Kentron Police Station in Yerevan and the Chief of the Yerevan Police, entitled "Assaults and insults of a public official; organisation of public events in violation of the procedure prescribed by law; mass disorder within the territory of Kentron Police Station", stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. officers of the Armenian police, having received an order, demanded the persons gathered at Freedom Square to vacate the square and to terminate the mass event.

The memorandum signed by the Chief of Kentron Police Station and the Chief of the Yerevan Police stated that the activists of the rally were brought in to Kentron Police Station in Yerevan, among them A.M., the applicant, D.A., M.A., V.H. and H.B.
From 7.20 to 7.40 p.m. on 1 March 2008 the investigator questioned the applicant as a witness.
The applicant was kept in a cell at Kentron Police Station until around 10 p.m. on 1 March 2008, when the investigator came to question him again.
At around 10.30 p.m. on 1 March 2008 the investigator drew up a record of the applicant's arrest by filling in the relevant template, indicating "10.30 p.m." as the time of the applicant's arrest.
On 2 March 2008, in the early morning, the applicant was transferred to police holding cells.

On 3 March 2008 the applicant was formally charged under Articles 225.1 § 2 and 316 § 2, as well as Articles 301 and 318 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code, within the scope of criminal case no. 62202608.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police officers demanded the participants in the demonstration at Freedom Square to give a possibility to verify the veracity of the information that they possessed arms and ammunition, and once again warned them to end the unlawful event, the applicant and other demonstrators, disobeying the police officers' lawful orders, committed life- and health-threatening assault on them.

On 4 March 2008 the applicant's lawyer filed a complaint with the Chief of the Special Investigative Service, alleging that the applicant had been unjustifiably taken to Kentron Police Station under the so-called procedure of "bringing-in", subjected to ill-treatment and then unlawfully kept there the whole day on 1 March 2008.

The applicant's lawyer's complaint of 4 March 2008 stated that the applicant's 72-hour arrest permitted by law had already expired, in violation of Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention, and it was still unclear on what evidence the charge against him was based.
On 4 March 2008 at 7 p.m. the applicant was brought before the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan which examined the investigator's application seeking to have him detained.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan decided to allow the investigator's application and order the applicant's detention for a period of two months.
On 5 March 2008 the applicant was transferred to Vardashen Remand Prison.

On 25 April 2008 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan extended the applicant's detention by two months, finding that it was still necessary to carry out a number of investigative measures and that, if he remained at large, the applicant could abscond, obstruct the proceedings, commit another offence and evade criminal responsibility.

On 26 June 2008 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan extended the applicant's detention by a further two months, finding that it was still necessary to carry out a number of investigative measures and that, if he remained at large, the applicant could abscond, obstruct the proceedings, commit another offence and evade criminal responsibility.

On 12 June 2008 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan under Article 290 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure, seeking to have the relevant police order which served as a basis for the police operation of 1 March 2008 declared unlawful and unfounded, and the ensuing police actions declared unlawful.

In his complaint of 12 June 2008, the applicant submitted that in the morning of 1 March 2008 armed police forces had suddenly invaded Freedom Square and started beating peaceful demonstrators, and that the police attack had been unjustified and failed to meet the requirements of Article 11 § 2 of the Convention.

In his complaint of 12 June 2008, the applicant submitted that the true purpose of the police operation was to launch political persecution of the supporters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan, including himself, by provoking the demonstrators to engage in clashes, creating artificial charges of resistance to police and punishing them for exercising their right to freedom of assembly and for their political opinion.
On 23 October 2008 the Yerevan Criminal Court found the applicant guilty under Article 235 § 4 and Article 316 §§ 1 and 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code.
The Yerevan Criminal Court sentenced the applicant under Article 235 § 4 of the Armenian Criminal Code to a fine in the amount of 400,000 Armenian drams.
The Yerevan Criminal Court sentenced the applicant under Article 316 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code to a fine in the amount of 500,000 Armenian drams.
The Yerevan Criminal Court sentenced the applicant under Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code to five years' imprisonment.

In his appeal of 10 November 2008, the applicant argued that the interference with his freedom of peaceful assembly had been unlawful, unjustified and accompanied with use of excessive force by the police.
At the end of November 2010 the applicant was released from prison after having served more than half of his sentence.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted President Robert Kocharyan as stating: "The unauthorised demonstrations were not terminated by the police for nine consecutive days only for one reason: I prohibited them to do so. The reason was the post-election recount and the appeal process. I believed that a dispersal of demonstrations would be perceived as an attempt by the authorities to undermine the recount or the appeal process."

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the campaign headquarters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan and the opposition Heritage Party both insisted that the objective of the measures of the morning of 1 March 2008 was, under the disguise of an inspection of the area, to terminate by force the peaceful demonstrations that had been ongoing for ten days, to remove the persons participating in the sit-in and to ban further demonstrations at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that not all the persons gathered at Freedom Square were purported criminals, and that the police operation directly resulted in the forcible termination of the demonstration, with demonstrators being chased far beyond Freedom Square.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) stated that the violations and shortcomings observed in the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election raised questions among a part of the Armenian public with regard to the credibility of the outcome of the election, and that this lack of public confidence was the basis for the peaceful protests – held without prior official notification – that ensued after the announcement of the preliminary results, and which were tolerated by the authorities for ten days.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) condemned the arrest and continuing detention of scores of persons, including more than 100 opposition supporters and three members of parliament, some of them on seemingly artificial and politically motivated charges, characterising this as a de facto crackdown on the opposition by the authorities.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) urged the Armenian authorities to guarantee freedom of assembly in both law and practice, in compliance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and to stop arbitrary arrests and detentions, as well as the ill-treatment of detainees, in particular during police custody.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that after nine days of peaceful demonstrations on Opera Square (Freedom Square), the national police and security forces tried to disperse the protesters on 1 March 2008, and that clashes occurred between the police and security forces and the demonstrators in front of Myasnikyan's monument and the French Embassy, which resulted in the death of eight persons.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the search operation reportedly started early Saturday morning at approximately 6.30 a.m., during which tents were taken down and people were beaten and injured, and that demonstrators started resisting and clashes broke out.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that on 13 March 2008 the Prosecutor General informed that over 95 persons had been arrested for having organized or participated in demonstrations and mass disturbances of public order, and that most of the arrested had been charged with disturbing public order, illegal possession of arms, incitement to violent acts, and resisting violently police arrest.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 9 May 2011 stated that over a hundred people were arrested in the context of the March 2008 events, virtually all of them opposition supporters, and many of them were subjected to criminal proceedings.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that opposition supporters began peaceful rallies on 20 February 2008 in Yerevan to protest against the election result and demand a rerun, and that on the evening of 1 March 2008, after eleven days of protest by opposition supporters, violence erupted when police moved into Freedom Square in central Yerevan to disperse the protesters camped out in tents, leaving eight people dead, including one police officer, and dozens injured.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that a state of emergency was declared on 1 March 2008, which imposed restrictions on the freedom of the media, freedom of assembly and political parties.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 expressed concern at the violent police crackdown on opposition demonstrations, leading to the death of eight citizens including one police officer, with over a hundred injured, and called for a prompt, thorough, transparent, independent and impartial investigation of the events of 1 March 2008, including an independent investigation of the police intervention during the dispersal of the demonstration.

By a letter of 27 March 2008 the Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police replied to the Chief of the Special Investigative Service's request of 10 March 2008, stating that the organisers and participants in the unauthorised rallies held between 20 and 29 February 2008 had, on numerous occasions, been informed about the unlawful nature of those events.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the operation was carried out between 7 and 7.30 a.m. and was followed by a search, as a result of which numerous specially adapted metal objects, arms, ammunition and Molotov cocktails were found.

According to a handwritten document entitled "the record of bringing-in", the applicant was "brought in" to Kentron Police Station on 1 March 2008 at around 6.30 a.m. by three police officers, E.R., H.S. and A.A., from 1 Grigor Lusavorich Street.

The record of bringing-in stated that the applicant was brought to Kentron Police Station "for organising unauthorised demonstrations at Freedom Square in support of Mr Ter-Petrosyan, resisting police officers and disobeying their lawful orders".
The applicant alleged that the record of bringing-in had never been presented to him.

Police officer E.R. reported to the Chief of Kentron Police Station that at around 7.30 a.m. on 1 March 2008, together with police officers H.S. and A.A., he brought the applicant in to Kentron Police Station from near Yerevan circus for having resisted police officers.

Another report addressed by police officer E.R. to the Chief of Kentron Police Station, signed by all three officers E.R., H.S. and A.A., stated that following an alert received on 1 March 2008, they were in the area of the unauthorised demonstration held at Freedom Square where the demonstrators were ordered to terminate the unauthorised demonstration and to clear the square.

Police officers E.R., H.S. and A.A. addressed several other reports to the Chief of Kentron Police Station with practically identical content, stating that following an alert received on 1 March 2008 they were in the area of the unauthorised demonstration held at Freedom Square where the demonstrators were ordered to terminate the unauthorised demonstration and to clear the square.

A memorandum signed by the Chief of Kentron Police Station in Yerevan and the Chief of the Yerevan Police, entitled "Assaults and insults of a public official; organisation of public events in violation of the procedure prescribed by law; mass disorder within the territory of Kentron Police Station", stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. officers of the Armenian police, having received an order, demanded the persons gathered at Freedom Square to vacate the square and to terminate the mass event.
At around 10.30 p.m. on 1 March 2008 the investigator drew up a record of the applicant's arrest by filling in the relevant template, indicating "10.30 p.m." as the time of the applicant's arrest.
The arrest record indicated "Articles 225.1 § 2 and 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code" as the provisions under which the applicant was suspected of having committed offences.

Police officers E.R., H.S. and A.A. stated during questioning on 2 March 2008 that certain police officers, over a loudspeaker, ordered those gathered at Freedom Square to terminate the unlawful and unauthorised demonstration and to leave, but they did not leave and some of them incited disobedience to the orders of the police officers and to continue the demonstration.

The charge against the applicant of 3 March 2008 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police officers demanded the participants in the demonstration at Freedom Square to give a possibility to verify the veracity of the information that they possessed arms and ammunition, and once again warned them to end the unlawful event, the applicant and other demonstrators, disobeying the police officers' lawful orders, committed life- and health-threatening assault on them.

On 12 June 2008 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan under Article 290 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure, seeking to have the relevant police order which served as a basis for the police operation of 1 March 2008 declared unlawful and unfounded, and the ensuing police actions declared unlawful.

On 8 July 2008 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan dismissed the applicant's complaint of 12 June 2008, finding that the relevant police order was not a decision or action prescribed by the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore could not be contested under Article 290 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan found on 8 July 2008 that the applicant's requests to quash the decisions in question and to discontinue the criminal proceedings could be lodged with a court only after they had been raised before a prosecutor, which the applicant had failed to do.
On 19 August 2008 the Criminal Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan of 8 July 2008 and dismissed the applicant's appeal.

The Criminal Court of Appeal found on 19 August 2008, relying on Article 290 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure, that the contested police order, the decision to institute criminal proceedings, as well as ordering the investigating authority to discontinue the criminal proceedings, were beyond the scope of judicial control over the investigation.

The Criminal Court of Appeal found on 19 August 2008 that Article 290 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure presupposed judicial control over pre-trial proceedings and therefore applied only to the period after a decision to institute such proceedings was taken.

On 5 August 2008 the investigator decided to drop the charges against the applicant under Article 225.1 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code, finding that it had been established by the investigation that the order issued by the police officers to the demonstrators on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. at Freedom Square was not to disperse but to allow them to inspect the area, and thus the applicant's actions did not contain elements of a crime prescribed by that Article.

Article 225.1 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that inciting disobedience to an order to terminate a public event held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law is punishable by a fine of between 300 and 500 times the minimum wage or detention of up to three months.

Article 316 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that non-life-threatening or non-health-threatening assault or threat of such assault on a public official or his or her next-of-kin, connected with the performance of his or her official duties, is punishable by a fine of between 300 and 500 times the minimum wage or detention of up to one month or imprisonment for a period not exceeding five years.

Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that a life-threatening or a health-threatening assault on a public official or his or her next-of-kin, connected with the performance of their duties, is punishable by imprisonment for a period from five to ten years.

Article 34 § 1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that a body of inquiry, an investigator and a prosecutor may arrest and question a person suspected of having committed an offence, as well as impose measures of compulsion and bring charges against such a person, on the grounds and in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Code.

Article 62 § 1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "Suspect", provides that a suspect is the person (a) who has been arrested upon a suspicion of having committed an offence; or (b) in whose respect, prior to bringing a charge, a decision has been adopted to impose a preventive measure.

Article 63 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) enumerates the rights enjoyed by a suspect, including the right to be informed about the reasons for his arrest and his rights as a suspect, to have a lawyer and to be questioned in his or her presence, to remain silent and to inform his next-of-kin – immediately and, in any event, not later than 12 hours after being taken into custody – of the place where he is held in custody and the grounds for his custody.

Article 128 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "The Notion of Arrest", provides that arrest is the taking of a person into custody, bringing him before the body of inquiry or the authority conducting the criminal proceedings, drawing up the relevant record and informing that person about it, for the purpose of preventing him or her from committing an offence or from fleeing after having committed an offence and with the aim of keeping that person in short-term custody in places and conditions defined by law.

Article 128 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that a person may be arrested (1) on an immediate suspicion of having committed an offence; or (2) on the basis of an arrest warrant issued by the prosecuting authority.

Article 129 § 1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "Arrest on an Immediate Suspicion of Having Committed an Offence", provides that a person suspected of having committed an offence may be arrested if (a) he was caught while committing a criminal act or immediately thereafter; (b) an eyewitness directly points him out as the perpetrator of a criminal act; (c) obvious traces linking him to a criminal act have been discovered on him, his clothes or other objects used by him, or in his home or vehicle; or (d) there are other grounds to suspect a person, who has made an attempt to flee from the crime scene or from the authority conducting criminal proceedings or who has no permanent residence or resides elsewhere or whose identity is unknown, of having committed an offence.

Article 129 § 2 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that an arrest on immediate suspicion of having committed an offence may not exceed 72 hours from the moment of taking into custody.

Article 131.1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "The Procedure for a Suspect's Arrest", provides that a record of a suspect's arrest must be drawn up within three hours of bringing him before the body of inquiry, the investigator or the prosecutor and a copy must be given to the arrested person upon his signature.

Article 131.1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that the record of a suspect's arrest must indicate the time when it was drawn up (date, hour and minute), the time, place, reason(s) and purpose of the arrest, the article of the Criminal Code under which a person is suspected of having committed an offence, the results of his personal search and other circumstances, including any declarations and requests by the arrested person.

Article 6 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) prescribes that "taking into custody" is the act which starts from the moment of a person's de facto and forcible deprivation of liberty when being arrested or detained or when enforcing a custodial sentence.

Article 153 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "Bringing-In", provides that bringing a person in is when a suspect, accused, defendant, convicted person, witness or victim, who fails to appear before the investigating authority without valid reasons, is forcibly taken to the body conducting the criminal proceedings in order to carry out procedural measures with his participation as prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, which may lead to the temporary restriction of rights and freedoms of the brought-in person.

Article 153 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that "bringing-in" is carried out upon a reasoned decision of the body of inquiry, the investigator, the prosecutor or the court.

Article 180 § 1 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "Procedure for examination of crime reports", provides that crime reports must be examined and decided upon immediately, while in cases where it is necessary to check whether there are lawful and sufficient grounds to institute a criminal case, within ten days following the receipt of such reports.

Article 180 § 2 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that within the period for examination of crime reports, additional documents, statements or other materials may be obtained; the scene of the incident may be inspected; persons may be brought in and subjected to a personal search if there are sufficient grounds for a suspicion that they have committed an offence; samples may be taken for inspection; and examinations may be ordered.

Article 103 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that actions and decisions of the authority conducting the criminal proceedings may be appealed against by the participants in the proceedings, in accordance with a procedure prescribed by the Code.

Article 103 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that appeal against actions and decisions of an investigator or an officer of a body of inquiry lies to the respective prosecutor, against actions and decisions of a prosecutor to a superior prosecutor, and against actions and decisions of a court to a superior court.

Article 103 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that in cases prescribed by the Code an appeal against actions and decisions of the prosecuting authority may be lodged with a court.

Article 290 §§ 1, 4 and 5 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), entitled "Contesting before a court unlawful and unfounded decisions and actions of a body of inquiry, an investigator, a prosecutor or bodies carrying out operative and intelligence measures", provides that such decisions and actions may be contested before a court by the suspect, the accused, the defence lawyer, the victim, the participants in the criminal proceedings and other persons whose rights and lawful interests were violated by those decisions and actions, if their complaints had not been granted by a prosecutor.

Article 290 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) provides that the complaint shall be examined by a single judge within ten days from its receipt, and if the complaint is found to be substantiated, the court shall adopt a decision obliging the body conducting the criminal proceedings to put an end to the violation of a person's rights and freedoms.

Section 2 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the concept of a public event includes peaceful assemblies, rallies, marches (parades) and demonstrations (including sit-ins).

Section 2 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that mass public events are those public events which have a hundred or more participants, and non-mass public events are those which have fewer than a hundred participants.

Section 7 §§ 1 and 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that everyone has the right to participate in public events, and that participants in a public event are not allowed to carry, use or apply weapons, ammunition, explosives, poisonous, inflammable or any other objects or substances which may harm the life, health or property of others.

Section 10 §§ 1, 2 and 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that, except for cases when a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event, mass public events may be held only after notifying the competent authority in writing.

Section 10 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that everyone has the right to hold non-mass public events without notifying the competent authority and without violating public order.

Section 10 § 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the organisers shall submit a written notification of the intention to hold a mass public event to the head of the local authority where the event is to be held or to the Mayor of Yerevan, if the public event is to be held in Yerevan, not later than five working days and not earlier than twenty days before the planned date of the event.

Section 12 § 8 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that, should the competent authority not take a decision banning the mass public event, the organisers shall have the right to hold the mass public event on the terms and conditions set forth in the notification.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to decide to terminate a public event and to order the organisers to terminate the event, by allowing them a reasonable time-limit to do so, if, inter alia, the mass public event is being held without notification, except for the cases in which a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the organiser, having received the order to terminate the event, is obliged to announce immediately the termination of the event and to take measures aimed at terminating the event within the time-limit fixed by the police.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to terminate forcibly a public event only if (a) the order to terminate an event is not immediately announced to the participants by the organiser; or (b) the order to terminate the public event has not been complied with within the fixed time-limit and its continuation poses a real threat to the life and health of others, State and public security, public order or public or private property.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police, before forcibly terminating an event, are obliged to inform the participants at least twice over a loudspeaker about the order to terminate the public event and to fix a reasonable time-limit for its termination, and that if the public event is not terminated within such a time-limit, the police are entitled to terminate the event forcibly, using lawful means.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the procedure for forcible termination shall not be applied if an outbreak of mass disorder takes place in the location where the public event is held, requiring implementation of urgent measures.

On 18 December 2009 the Court of Cassation of Armenia adopted a decision in an unrelated criminal case, examining questions concerning initial deprivation of liberty under the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999).

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 pointed out that there were two procedures for depriving a person of his liberty on suspicion of having committed an offence under the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999), namely "arrest" (Articles 128-133) and "detention" (Articles 137-142).

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 stated that the arrest procedure under Article 128 of the Armenian Code of Criminal Procedure (1999) consisted of four consecutive actions: (a) the de facto deprivation of a person's liberty; (b) bringing him before the competent authority; (c) drawing up a record of his arrest; and (d) informing him about that record.

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 stated that a person could obtain the status of an "arrestee" only after the completion of the fourth and final action, namely after he was informed about the record of his arrest before the prosecuting authority.

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 stated that if the relevant authority continued and completed the arrest procedure in respect of a person brought before it, then the start of the arrest period would be calculated from the moment that person had been taken into custody, albeit retroactively.

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 concluded that the procedures for depriving a person of liberty on a suspicion of having committed an offence were not limited to "arrest" and "detention" but also included the procedure of taking into custody and bringing before the relevant authority, and that a person deprived of his liberty could also have an initial legal status which could be conditionally called the status of a "brought-in person".

The Court of Cassation's decision of 18 December 2009 stated that persons in such situations should enjoy the rights guaranteed by the Constitution and the Convention, including knowing the reasons for their deprivation of liberty, having access to a lawyer and maintaining silence.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that in the period preceding 1 March 2008 intelligence information was received by the Armenian Police and the National Security Service that the demonstrators gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square had in their possession firearms, ammunition, clubs, rods and other objects for the purpose of causing physical injuries and violence.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. police officers demanded the persons gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square to allow them to verify the above information by inspecting the area, and that this demand was announced out loud several times.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that some of the people gathered at Freedom Square, including the applicant, had already been informed several hours in advance about the planned police operation.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that the applicant, in front of the statue of Hovhannes Tumanyan, hit police officer A.Arsh. twice on the head with a stick, causing light damage to his health accompanied by a brief deterioration of health, after which he disappeared in the crowd.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that police officer A.Aru. saw the act committed by the applicant against police officer A.Arsh. and continued his duty in the area near the Yerevan Press Building situated at Arshakunyats Street, where he once again noticed the applicant and tried to bring him in.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that the applicant, disobeying police officer A.Aru.'s lawful order to appear at the police station, assaulted him in a non-health-threatening way by pushing, pulling and kicking him, and tried to escape in a random taxi.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that police officers A.A., E.R. and H.S., who were on duty in the same area, noticed the incident and brought the applicant in to Kentron Police Station, during which a bladed weapon – a knife – fell from the applicant's pocket, as well as two mobile telephones and a bunch of keys.

In his appeal of 10 November 2008, the applicant argued that the trial court had failed to make any assessment of the police actions at Freedom Square, including their lawfulness and proportionality, without which the charge against him could not receive a fair determination.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted the OSCE/ODIHR report as stating: "From 21 February to early morning on 1 March protesters held a peaceful, though not formally authorised, assembly (and tent camp) in Freedom Square in Yerevan and conducted numerous peaceful processions. Speakers at the assembly announced that their aim was to annul and repeat the election. Until 1 March, the authorities overall tolerated the protests."

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted President Robert Kocharyan as stating: "The unauthorised demonstrations were not terminated by the police for nine consecutive days only for one reason: I prohibited them to do so. The reason was the post-election recount and the appeal process. I believed that a dispersal of demonstrations would be perceived as an attempt by the authorities to undermine the recount or the appeal process."

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 intervention was justified with the argument that on 29 February the police and the National Security Service had received intelligence information according to which arms were building up at Freedom Square, and that in order to render the situation harmless, in the morning of 1 March the police undertook an operation intended to seize those socially-dangerous materials.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the campaign headquarters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan and the opposition Heritage Party both insisted that the objective of the measures of the morning of 1 March 2008 was, under the disguise of an inspection of the area, to terminate by force the peaceful demonstrations that had been ongoing for ten days, to remove the persons participating in the sit-in and to ban further demonstrations at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report noted contradictions in the statements released by the Prosecutor General's Office, including that the request lodged by the Prosecutor General on 4 March 2008 stated "the objective of the police was to carry out an operation aimed at seizing arms, which deteriorated into a clash", while the press release issued by the Prosecutor General's Office on 1 March stated "the objective of the police was to terminate forcibly the assembly at around 6 a.m. on 1 March".

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report raised the question of how it happened that at around 6.30 a.m. on 1 March 2008, in a matter of just minutes, the police was able to mobilise numerous units wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons, if the only objective was to perform an inspection of the area.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report noted concerns over the confiscation of the videotapes of two media outlets and the smashing of the camcorder of a third media outlet, all of which were videotaping in the area of Freedom Square in the morning of 1 March 2008, and that a freelance photographer of Aravot daily was beaten and the photos he had taken were taken away.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that in the morning of 1 March 2008 and later on the same day in the vicinity of the French Embassy, no shots were fired during the first half of the day and no firearms were used by the demonstrators.
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that on 29 February 2008 President Robert Kocharyan stated that among available solutions was the "cleaning of the Square" by the police.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that while it is true that every day prior to 1 March the police announced over loudspeakers that the demonstration was unlawful and ordered the demonstrators to end it, no such order was made in the morning of 1 March 2008 and no time-limit was given to the demonstrators to end the demonstration as required by section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that there were two police cordons at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008: one right on the square and the other one along the four adjacent streets, and that the purpose of those cordons was to keep everyone out so that the demonstration ended.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that not all the persons gathered at Freedom Square were purported criminals, and that the police operation directly resulted in the forcible termination of the demonstration, with demonstrators being chased far beyond Freedom Square.
The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that to date, not a single criminal case had been initiated against any police officer, even for excessive use of physical force and of special means.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) stated that the violations and shortcomings observed in the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election raised questions among a part of the Armenian public with regard to the credibility of the outcome of the election, and that this lack of public confidence was the basis for the peaceful protests – held without prior official notification – that ensued after the announcement of the preliminary results, and which were tolerated by the authorities for ten days.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) deplored the clashes between the police and the protesters and the escalation of violence on 1 March 2008 which resulted in 10 deaths and about 200 people being injured, and stated that the exact circumstances that led to the tragic events of 1 March, as well as the manner in which they were handled by the authorities, including the imposition of a state of emergency in Yerevan from 1 to 20 March 2008 and the alleged excessive use of force by the police, should be the subject of a credible independent investigation.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) condemned the arrest and continuing detention of scores of persons, including more than 100 opposition supporters and three members of parliament, some of them on seemingly artificial and politically motivated charges, characterising this as a de facto crackdown on the opposition by the authorities.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) urged the Armenian authorities to guarantee freedom of assembly in both law and practice, in compliance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and to stop arbitrary arrests and detentions, as well as the ill-treatment of detainees, in particular during police custody.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) called for an independent, transparent and credible inquiry into the events of 1 March 2008 and the circumstances that led to them, including the alleged excessive use of force by the police and violence by the protesters, and for the release of persons detained on seemingly artificial and politically motivated charges or who did not personally commit any violent acts or serious offences.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1620 (2008) stated that the cases under Articles 300 and 225 of the Armenian Criminal Code should be dropped unless there is strong evidence that the accused have personally committed acts of violence or ordered, abetted or assisted the committing of such acts, and that a verdict based solely on a single police testimony without corroborating evidence is not acceptable.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1643 (2009), adopted on 27 January 2009, stated that a significant number of prosecution cases and convictions in relation to the events of 1 and 2 March 2008 in Armenia was based solely on police testimony, without substantial corroborating evidence.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1643 (2009) considered that the charges against a significant number of persons, especially those charged under Articles 225, paragraph 3, and 300 of the Armenian Criminal Code and those based solely on police evidence, could have been politically motivated.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that practically all the persons who had been detained by law enforcement officers on 1 March 2008 alleged that they had been physically ill-treated at the time of their apprehension, even though they apparently had not offered resistance, with the ill-treatment consisting mainly of truncheon blows, kicks and punches to the body and head, and being pushed to the ground and dragged into a police vehicle.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that in some cases the beating had apparently continued during transportation to police establishments and upon arrival there, and that according to several of the persons alleging ill-treatment, some of the law enforcement officials involved were wearing masks and did not have any form of identification on their clothing.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that the delegation received a few allegations of physical ill-treatment at the time of questioning by the police, consisting essentially of slaps, punches, kicks and truncheon blows, apparently inflicted with the purpose of obtaining confessions or information implicating other persons.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment's report stated that certain of the persons who made allegations of ill-treatment were found on examination by a medical member of the delegation to display physical marks or conditions consistent with their allegations, and that the medical documentation at the penitentiary establishments visited also contained descriptions of various injuries observed by prison doctors during the initial examination of a number of persons admitted in the two weeks preceding the delegation's visit.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that after nine days of peaceful demonstrations on Opera Square (Freedom Square), the national police and security forces tried to disperse the protesters on 1 March 2008, and that clashes occurred between the police and security forces and the demonstrators in front of Myasnikyan's monument and the French Embassy, which resulted in the death of eight persons.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the Head of Police explained that the police had received information that the demonstrators were arming themselves with weapons and ammunition, and that the initial intent was also to move them to another location in the city to avoid problems of public transport and sanitation.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the search operation reportedly started early Saturday morning at approximately 6.30 a.m., during which tents were taken down and people were beaten and injured, and that demonstrators started resisting and clashes broke out.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that it seemed clear that excessive use of force was used by police and the security forces, as confirmed by the sheer number of injured persons and passing civilians registered in the hospitals as well as found in places of detention, having beating marks, concussion and open scars on their skulls.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that detainees claimed that the police had used excessive force in connection with arrest, and that it seemed that beating took place in a number of cases at the time of arrest and during transportation of the apprehended to the different precincts.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the prosecutors had consistently brought the same charges irrespective of the person's actual doing and involvement, regularly invoking Article 225 § 3, Article 316 and Article 300 of the Armenian Criminal Code, and had applied standardized language in the charges against those arrested.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the judges seemed not to have entered into a serious test of the charges, the legality of the apprehension and the proportionality of deprivation of liberty, and that the courts seemed to have routinely granted pre-trial detention of two months to allow the prosecutor to investigate further and prepare the charges and the criminal case.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Summary of Findings of 29 September 2008 stated that prosecution cases against 19 persons were based solely on police testimony, and that many interlocutors considered that the principle of equality of arms was not being applied in practice, and that the resort to fast trial proceedings in a number of cases – certain of which had lasted less than 30 minutes – gave rise to questions.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Summary of Findings of 29 September 2008 stated that to date, no law enforcement officials had been charged in connection with the 1 March 2008 events.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that opposition supporters began peaceful rallies on 20 February 2008 in Yerevan to protest against the election result and demand a rerun, and that on the evening of 1 March 2008, after eleven days of protest by opposition supporters, violence erupted when police moved into Freedom Square in central Yerevan to disperse the protesters camped out in tents, leaving eight people dead, including one police officer, and dozens injured.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 expressed concern at the violent police crackdown on opposition demonstrations, leading to the death of eight citizens including one police officer, with over a hundred injured, and called for a prompt, thorough, transparent, independent and impartial investigation of the events of 1 March 2008, including an independent investigation of the police intervention during the dispersal of the demonstration.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that statements taken from demonstrators and bystanders suggested that the first police action in the early morning of 1 March 2008 against the Freedom Square tent encampment entailed excessive use of force, without warning and in the absence, at the start, of resistance.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to the first deputy police chief A.M., the police had arrived at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 to conduct a search, acting on information that demonstrators had been arming themselves with metal rods, and possibly firearms, in preparation for committing acts of violent protest, and that initially a group of 25-30 police officers, including experts and investigators, were sent to do the search.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to the first deputy police chief A.M., when the group tried to conduct the search, the protesters turned aggressive and resisted police with wooden sticks and iron bars, resulting in injuries to several policemen, and that more police had to be deployed and had to use force to disperse the crowd, with the operation lasting about 30 minutes and 10 policemen sustaining injuries.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that several witnesses interviewed separately by Human Rights Watch consistently described that some time shortly after 6 a.m. on 1 March 2008, while it was still dark, hundreds of Special Forces police in riot armour, with helmets, plastic shields, and rubber truncheons, started approaching Freedom Square from Tumanyan Street and Mashtots Avenue, surrounded the square and stood there for a few minutes.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to Mr Ter-Petrosyan's account, he addressed the protesters asking them to step back from the police line and then to stay where they were and wait for instructions from the police, and also warned the police that there were women and children among the demonstrators.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to multiple witnesses, even before Mr Ter-Petrosyan finished his address, police advanced towards the demonstrators in several lines, beating their truncheons against their plastic shields, making no audible demand for anyone to disperse nor giving any indication of the purpose of their presence, and then without any warning, riot police attacked the demonstrators, using rubber truncheons, iron sticks, and electric shock batons.
Human Rights Watch's report stated that as a result of the early morning police actions on Freedom Square on 1 March 2008, 31 people were officially reported to be injured, including six policemen.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that the police claimed that after the demonstrators were dispersed they found a stock of real and makeshift weapons, including three guns, 15 grenades, two bullet cases and 138 bullets of various calibres, plastic explosives, a big number of makeshift weapons, syringes and drugs, but that all witnesses and victims interviewed by Human Rights Watch claimed that the alleged arms cache was planted after the demonstration was dispersed.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that the chairman of the ad hoc parliamentary commission established to investigate the 1 March 2008 events told Human Rights Watch in January 2009 that he had not seen any evidence linking the arms cache to the demonstration's participants or organizers.
